sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Differential Diagnosis
sections.description: This section outlines the patient’s presenting symptoms, physical findings, and the early diagnostic considerations that guided initial management.
subtopics: History of present illness – progressive neck swelling, proximal weakness, and dysphagia
Relevant negative history – absence of drug exposures, infections, or known angioedema triggers
Physical examination findings – neck edema, nailfold microhaemorrhages, peri‑ungual erythema, thigh rash, and hip flexor weakness
Initial imaging (neck CT) and its interpretation – diffuse strap‑muscle edema suggesting Ludwig’s angina
First‑line differential diagnoses in the emergency/ENT setting:
• Deep neck space infection (Ludwig’s angio‑itis)
• Histamine‑mediated angioedema
• Bradykinin‑mediated (hereditary/acquired C1‑esterase inhibitor) angioedema
• Non‑infectious inflammatory conditions (e.g., inflammatory myopathy, vasculitis)
Rationale for shifting the focus from infectious to immunologic causes

sections.section_title: Dermatomyositis: Pathophysiology, Clinical Spectrum, and the Role of Anti‑SAE1 Antibodies
sections.description: Provides the necessary background on idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, emphasizing the mechanisms and typical manifestations of dermatomyositis, with a focus on the anti‑SAE1 antibody subtype.
subtopics: Definition of dermatomyositis and its classification within idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
Key pathogenic mechanisms:
• Complement‑mediated microangiopathy (C5b‑9 deposition)
• Autoantibody‑driven immune dysregulation
• Role of sumoylation and the small ubiquitin‑like modifier‑activating enzyme (SAE) in disease
Clinical hallmarks:
• Cutaneous signs (Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash, V‑neck/holster sign, peri‑ungual telangiectasia)
• Proximal muscle weakness and elevated CK
• Extramuscular involvement (interstitial lung disease, dysphagia, cardiac, malignancy risk)
Epidemiology and typical age distribution
Anti‑SAE1 antibody phenotype:
• Frequency and associated clinical features (prominent skin disease, dysphagia, ILD)
• Comparative data on edema/angioedema prevalence in SAE1‑positive vs. other myositis antibodies
Why edema can mimic angioedema – inflammatory edema from myositis versus histamine/bradykinin pathways

sections.description: Details the step‑by‑step investigations performed, how each result narrowed the differential, and the final synthesis leading to the diagnosis of anti‑SAE1 dermatomyositis.
subtopics: Laboratory panel:
• Creatine kinase and muscle enzyme trends
• Liver enzymes and LDH as markers of muscle injury
• Inflammatory markers (CRP, WCC)
• Autoimmune serologies – ANA pattern, myositis‑specific antibody panel (SAE1 positivity)
• Complement levels and C1‑esterase inhibitor testing to exclude hereditary/acquired angioedema
Imaging studies:
• Neck CT – pattern of soft‑tissue edema without abscess
• Chest CT and PFTs – evaluation for ILD and aspiration changes
• MRI of thighs – muscle edema and distribution consistent with active myositis
• FDG‑PET – diffuse muscular uptake, exclusion of occult malignancy
Procedural diagnostics:
• Nailfold capillaroscopy – microhaemorrhages indicating microvascular involvement
• Muscle biopsy – perifascicular necrosis, C5b‑9 deposition, histologic confirmation of dermatomyositis
Integration of findings:
• How elevated CK, SAE1 antibody, characteristic biopsy, and imaging co‑here
• Ruling out alternative diagnoses (infection, neuromuscular junction disorders, drug reactions)
Diagnostic criteria applied (e.g., 2017 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for DM)

sections.description: Explores the evidence‑based treatment plan, including acute management of severe muscle inflammation and long‑term immunosuppression, with justification for each medication choice.
subtopics: Acute phase treatment:
• High‑dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day × 3) – rapid control of inflammation and airway risk
• Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) loading dose – mechanisms (Fc blockade, complement inhibition) and indications in refractory/ severe DM
Steroid tapering protocol – transition to oral prednisone and taper schedule
Steroid‑sparing agents:
• Mycophenolate mofetil – mechanism, dosing, advantages in ILD‑prone patients
• Rituximab – B‑cell depletion rationale, dosing regimen, evidence in refractory DM
Agents deliberately avoided and why:
• Methotrexate – potential for pulmonary toxicity in a patient with early ILD
• Azathioprine & tacrolimus – alternative options discussed
Infection prophylaxis:
• Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis – initial TMP‑SMX, switch to nebulized pentamidine after hemolysis
Supportive care:
• Nutritional support via nasogastric tube during dysphagia
• Physical therapy and rehabilitation for muscle strength recovery
Monitoring during therapy – CK trends, liver function, immunoglobulin levels, infection surveillance

sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory, long‑term monitoring plan, and key take‑away points for clinicians encountering similar presentations.
subtopics: Short‑term response:
• Improvement in neck edema, CK normalization, and gradual return of hip flexor strength
• Persistent dysphagia requiring NG‑tube for 2 months
Long‑term outcome:
• Full muscle strength recovery, resolution of swelling, and discontinuation of prednisone by 7 months
• Residual restrictive pattern on PFTs – attribution to baseline physiology vs. residual disease
Imaging follow‑up – CT chest showing resolution of aspiration‑related changes
Malignancy surveillance strategy:
• Risk stratification based on IMACS guidelines (high‑risk features)
• Planned GI endoscopy, periodic imaging, and symptom‑driven work‑up
Key educational points:
1. Neck or facial edema can be a manifestation of inflammatory myopathy, not just angioedema.
2. Early CK measurement and careful skin examination are vital in atypical swelling.
3. Anti‑SAE1 antibodies correlate with cutaneous disease and dysphagia; they do not protect against edema.
4. Multimodal immunosuppression (steroids, IVIG, steroid‑sparing agents) can achieve remission even in severe presentations.
5. Systematic malignancy screening is mandatory in dermatomyositis, especially with high‑risk serology.
Future directions – emerging therapies (Janus‑kinase inhibitors, anti‑IFNα/β antibodies) and their potential role in SAE1‑positive disease
